passages.original: » Verbum Hebraicum SABAIM (D\OU7), quod Aquila et Symmachus ita ut scriptum est transtulerunt, LXX captivitatem interpretati sunt, quod melius captivos significat. Sabaim autem gens trans Indiam dicitur, de qua fuit et regina Saba, quae venit sa- pientiam audire Salomonis (III Reg.X), de quibus et Isaias loquitur : Et Sabaim viri excelsi ad te trans-ibunt (Isa.XLV, 14). Unde et thus venire perbi- betur, dicente Virgilio (AEneid. lib. I) : licet quidam Sabaeos, Arabes suspicentur. Promit- tunt ergo sibi Judaei, imo somniant, quod in ulti- mo tempore congregentur a Domino, et reducan- tur in Jerusalem. Nec hac felicitate contenti, ipsum Deum suis manibus Romanorum filios et filias asse- runt traditurum, ut vendant eos Judaei, non Persis et AEthiopibus et caeteris nationibus quae vicinae sunt;
passages.english: The Hebrew word SABAIM, which Aquila and Symmachus rendered just as it is written, the Seventy translated as "captivity", which would better signify "captives". Now Sabaim is said to be a nation beyond India, from which also came the queen of Saba, who came to hear the wisdom of Solomon (3 Kings 10), and of whom Isaiah also speaks: "And the Sabaim, men of stature, shall pass over to you" (Isaiah 45:14). From there too frankincense is said to come, as Virgil says (Aeneid, book 1): although some suppose the Sabaeans to be Arabs. So the Jews promise themselves, or rather dream, that in the last time they will be gathered by the Lord and led back to Jerusalem. And not content with this good fortune, they assert that God himself will hand over the sons and daughters of the Romans into their hands, so that the Jews may sell them, not to the Persians and Ethiopians and the other nations that are neighbours,
passages.notes: The Hebrew in parentheses after SABAIM is garbled in the scan ("D\OU7") and has been omitted. The Virgil quotation itself seems to have dropped out after "dicente Virgilio"; presumably it is Aeneid 1.416-417, on the Sabaean incense. The sentence breaks off and continues in the following passage ("but to the Sabaeans, a very distant nation").
